content: Complications and societal disruption can be minimized through effective pandemic response strategies. During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, it was observed that measuring attack rates and case-fatality ratios early in a pandemic can be challenging. This difficulty arises due to variations in care-seeking behaviors and testing practices. Not everyone with an illness seeks medical care, and not all individuals are tested or diagnosed with pandemic influenza. Consequently, severe cases are more likely to be reported, which can lead to an overestimation of case hospitalization or case-fatality ratios. Pre-pandemic planning tools have been updated and enhanced based on the lessons learned from the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. The Pandemic Severity Index from the 2007 guidance has been replaced with the Pandemic Severity Assessment Framework (PSAF). PSAF incorporates multiple clinical and epidemiologic indicators to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the transmissibility and clinical severity of an emerging pandemic. These indicators include secondary household attack rates, school attack rates, workplace attack rates, community attack rates, and rates of emergency department and outpatient visits for influenza-like illness (ILI). When a pandemic begins, whether in the United States or elsewhere, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) conducts an initial assessment of viral transmissibility and clinical severity using these PSAF measures. This assessment helps guide the response of affected jurisdictions and prepares other regions to respond. Although data are limited during the first 3-4 weeks after the emergence of a pandemic virus, these early data are compiled into a broad, preliminary assessment. The CDC uses PSAF scores for viral transmissibility and clinical severity to categorize the pandemic into one of four assessment quadrants. Depending on the surveillance capacity in the location where the novel virus emerges and begins to spread, it may take 4-8 weeks or longer to gather sufficient data for a more refined assessment of the evolving pandemic. Once adequate data are available, the refined assessment is used to more accurately characterize the clinical severity and transmissibility of the pandemic virus. These initial and refined assessments of pandemic severity are utilized, in collaboration with state and local public health partners, to guide the implementation of nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). Additional information about PSAF is available in supplementary materials. The 2017 update to the guidelines consists of three separate documents: this report and two supplementary documents. This report provides a brief introduction to pandemic influenza and NPIs, describes the 2007 strategy and the purpose of the updates (particularly following the 2009 H1N1 pandemic), outlines the methods used to develop this update, and discusses the evidence considered for NPI use during an influenza pandemic. It also presents the CDC's NPI recommendations and highlights key areas for further NPI research. The two supplementary documents contain more specific and detailed information about pandemic influenza and NPIs.
